title: Why Empordà tastes the way it does

lede.text: A cold, dry wind from the north often gusts at over 120 km/h across Empordà's vineyards. It keeps the grapes healthy until harvest, and it shaped which varieties grow here.

chapters.title: The far north-east corner of Catalonia
paras: Empordà sits in the far north-east of Catalonia. The production zone takes in 55 municipalities in two separate areas: 35 in the Alt Empordà and 20 in the Baix Empordà.

The Alt Empordà is tucked below the Rodes and Alberes ranges, in an arc from Cap de Creus to the Garrotxa d'Empordà. The Pyrenees close it in to the north. The Mediterranean lies to the east, and the plain opens to the south.
The Baix Empordà is bounded by the Montgrí massif in the north and the Gavarres massif in the south-west. The sea is to the east. The Pyrenees reach close to 1500 m, while the Gavarres peak at 535 m.
Vines grow from sea level up to a maximum of 260 m.

chapters.title: The wind that shaped the vineyards
paras: The climate is Mediterranean, with about 600 mm of rain a year and an annual mean of 14 to 16 °C. Winters are mild with few frosts. Summers are hot but softened by sea breezes.
That wind is the Tramuntana, the most characteristic feature of the climate. It clears the excess damp that can build up now and then in the wettest seasons, which keeps disease away.

Growers adapted to it long ago by choosing varieties with sturdier stems, such as Garnacha and Cariñena in their white, red and pink forms. They still dominate the vineyards today. On the plain, tall cypress trees, many of them centuries old, stand along the northern edge of fields as windbreaks. They bring a biodiversity that touches the primary aromas of the wines, with herbaceous and balsamic notes. In the coastal hills, dry-stone terraces show how the Tramuntana has set the lie of the vineyards for centuries. They already appear on the Cassini map of 1747.

Near the coast the sea tempers winter cold and keeps summer heat from spiking. This favours slow ripening, which gives the wines a distinctive elegance. Further inland the sea matters less, and the gap between day and night temperatures helps the grapes build colour, tannin and aroma. The wines there have deep colour and character, with high ageing potential.

The Winkler and Amerine scale sorts wine regions into five bands by their summer heat, and the area sits in the middle one, region III. That suits medium and long-cycle varieties and makes it well suited to natural sweet wines.

chapters.title: Many soils in a small space
paras: Few places pack so many soil types into so small an area. Most vines grow on poor, light soils that drain well and are acid to neutral. Most of the ground is sandy and low in organic matter.

In the mountains and mountain plains, granite and sandy soils sit beside slate soils, with a few limy (calcareous) patches. Wines from granite and from the gently sloping gravel-and-clay ground show great tension and acidity, with moderate colour and tannin.

Wines from slate and schist are different. They are high in alcohol and structured, with deep colour and firm tannins. Most become long-aged reds that taste mineral and spicy, or long-lived whites of medium alcohol that are rich on the palate. The same ground also gives liqueur wines from slightly overripe grapes, such as Garnacha and Moscatel del Empordà.

On the plain, soils are mostly alluvial: marl and clay in places, conglomerate and sandstone in others. Still wines from there are light, balsamic and silky. They make young whites, rosados (rosés) and reds that are fruity and fresh, with balanced acidity.
Producers know each kind of ground and have learned to complement their wines with grapes from parcels on different soils.

chapters.title: From fresh whites to century-old soleras
paras: Garnacha has a local name here. Lledoner negre is Garnacha Tinta, and Lledoner roig is a reddish Garnacha of Empordà. The recommended grapes are Garnacha and Cariñena in their white, red and black forms, with Macabeo and Moscatel de Alejandría. Many other grapes are grown, Syrah and Chardonnay among them.

The range is wide. Whites, rosados and reds can each be fermented or aged in wood, in whole or in part, and a wine partly aged in wood must spend at least 25% of its ageing there. A white called brisado is fermented with all its skins, pulp and pips, and sometimes the stalks, at least until fermentation ends. Needle wines (vinos de aguja) are lightly fizzy, with 1 to 2.5 bar of pressure. Sparkling wines are made by the traditional method and spend at least 9 months on their lees, the spent yeast, in the same bottle where the second fermentation happened.

Liqueur wines and wines from overripe grapes are deeply rooted here. The liqueur wines are fortified with wine spirit. Garnacha del Empordà is a liqueur wine from overripe grapes of at least 90% Garnacha, with 15 to 20% alcohol. It is called Ámbar when made from white or red Garnacha, and Rubí when made from Garnacha Tinta. It is usually aged in soleras, where its age counts as the average of the different fractions. Some soleras are more than a century old.

Moscatel del Empordà is a liqueur wine from overripe grapes, at least 90% Moscatel de Alejandría or Moscatel de Grano Menudo. Its fermentation is stopped by adding wine spirit, for 15 to 18% alcohol. Garnacha and Moscatel del Empordà may carry the words vino dulce natural (natural sweet wine) when the must is very rich in sugar. Mistelas, white and black, are liqueur wines made by adding wine spirit to the must. For the black one, the spirit goes in before fermentation has started. Vino dulce del Empordà is partly fermented and then fortified. Wines from overripe grapes (vino de uvas sobremaduradas) come from grapes left to overripen until they reach at least 18% natural alcohol. Rancio del Empordà is made in two forms, a still wine and a liqueur wine with wine spirit added. Both come from oxidative ageing for at least 2 years.

The Benedictine monastery of Sant Pere de Rodes was founded on Cap de Creus at the end of the 9th century. It promoted vines along the coast. A record kept by its cellar monk in 1420 lists vineyards on Cap de Creus, with the Moscatel vines ranked as the most prized. In 1779 the Baron de Bourgoing praised the sweet wines of Empordà and described its wine as halfway between Jerez and Frontignan.

terms.text: Also written vino novell. It may only be sold with its harvest year on the label. It is bottled before 31 January of the season the grapes were picked and may ship from an agreed date in November.
It may only be sold with its harvest year on the label. It is bottled during the harvest year and/or from 20 December of the year the grapes were picked.
Aged for at least 12 months in oak barrels of at most 330 litres.
For reds, at least 24 months of ageing with at least 6 months in oak barrels. For whites and rosados, at least 18 months with at least 6 months in oak. The barrels hold at most 330 litres.

For reds, at least 36 months with at least 12 in oak barrels and the rest in bottle. For whites and rosados, at least 24 months with at least 6 in oak and the rest in bottle. For sparkling wines, at least 15 months from bottling for the second fermentation to disgorging.

For reds, at least 60 months with at least 18 in oak barrels and the rest in bottle. For whites and rosados, at least 48 months with at least 6 in oak. For sparkling wines, at least 30 months from bottling for the second fermentation to disgorging.

Aged oxidatively in oak. Crianza means 3 years with at least 1 in oak. Reserva means 5 years with at least 4 in oak. Gran reserva means 8 years with at least 6 in oak. Vieja reserva means over 10 years in oak.
For Garnacha del Empordà aged in barrels by the solera system. The average age of its fractions must be at least 2 years, and the other ageing terms may not be used.
Fermented in wooden vessels of at most 600 litres.
Allowed when the wine's information states how many months or years it spent in wooden vessels (for roble, oak vessels).
For Garnacha and Moscatel del Empordà made from must very rich in sugar.
For wines and liqueur wines whose ageing has given them a rancio taste. A rancio with more than 45 g/L of sugar may be called rancio dulce.
Brut nature under 3 g/L of sugar. Extra brut 0 to 6. Brut under 12. Extra seco 12 to 17. Seco 17 to 32. Semi seco 32 to 50. Dulce over 50.
Seco up to 4 g/L of sugar. Semiseco 4 to 12. Semidulce 12 to 45. Dulce 45 and over.
The local names Lledoner negre, roig, blanc and pelut are recommended on the labels of wines that contain those grapes.
A grape may be named when at least 85% of the wine comes from it. A vintage year may be shown when at least 85% of the grapes were picked that year.
Estate bottled. For wine made only from grapes picked in vineyards the winery works, and made entirely on the estate.
